div.head: Hard-real-time schedulability analysis is carried out based on the assumption that the worst-case execution time (WCET) of each task is known. Cycle-stealing Direct Memory Access (DMA) I/O steals bus cycles from an executing program and prolongs the execution time of the program. Because of the dificulty in bounding the inte@erence on the executing program, cycle-stealing DMA I/O is often disabled in hard-real-time systems. This paper presents an analytical method for bounding the WCET of a program executing concurrently with cycle-stealing DMA I/O. This is an extension of our previous work [3] which bounded
div.p: the WCET of a straight-line sequence of instructions when cycle-stealing operations are allowed. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method with experiments on several programs.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In a hard-real-time system, the failure of a time-critical task to produce its result by its deadline is considered to be a fatal fault. Much of the research in hard-real-time scheduling theory carries out schedulability analysis based on the assumption that the worst-case execution time (WCET) of each program is known. To bound the WCET of a program, the dynamic execution of the program and interactions between the program and other activities in the system must be considered.

Mok e E al. [5] implemented a timing tool that finds the worst-case execution paths of assembly language programs and bounds their WCETs. Pusher and Koza 191 invented several new language constructs to let programmers provide information about the execution frequency constraints for a statement. Gupta and Gopinath [ 2 ] introduced techniques for identifying correlations among various statements within a program. Zhang, Burns and Nicholson [ 111 bounded the WCET of a program executed in a two-stage instruction pipeline. Lim et al. [4] extended the original work [7] to account for the effect of caching and pipelining execution on RISC processors. All the above methods assume no interaction between the executing program and other activities such as DMA U 0 in the system.
Jen-Yao Chung P.O. Box 704 IBM T. J. Watson Research Center Yorktown Heights, NY 10598, USA j ychung @ watson.ibm.com

This paper presents a method for bounding the WCET of an assembly language program executing concurrently with cycle-stealing DMA UO. A DMA controller (DMAC) transfers data between the main memory and I/O devices with minimal CPU involvement. It operates either in the burst mode or in the cycle-stealing mode. A DMAC that operates in the cycle-stealing mode transfers databy "stealing" bus cycles from an executing program. The cycle-stealing operation allows the concurrent execution of the CPU and the DMAC. It also retards the progress of the executing program and extends its execution time. Traditionally, the WCET of a program that executes concurrently with a cycle-stealing DMA U 0 operation has been predicted in a pessimistic approach; it is predicted as the sum of the WCET of the program when it executes alone and the WCET of the U 0 operation when it is done alone. Our previous work (Huang and Liu [3]) bounded the WCET of a sequence of instructions when cycle-stealing operations are allowed. In this paper we extend the previous work to bound the WCET of straight-line structures, loop structures, and conditional structures, the three basic structures of a program. An experiment designed to demonstrate the static and dynamic improvement from the pessimistic approach is described.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 describes a commonly used machine model. Section 3 describes the techniques for bounding the WCET of the three basic structures. The results of experiments that compare the performance of our analytical method and the pessimistic approach are presented in Section 4. Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future work.

div.head: The Machine Model
div.p: Figure 1 shows the architecture of the adopted machine model. In this model, the DMAC operates in the cyclestealing mode, and it shares the same U 0 bus with the CPU. The bus controller allows only one bus master at any time. As a result, either the CPU or the DMAC, but not both, can hold the bus and transfer data at the same time. Our analytical method is applicable only for systems that have no cache memory and pipelining execution, does not access the bus when it is in an E cycle. We assume that the CPU is a synchronous one, i.e., each machine cycle is triggered by the processor clock.

The bus controller uses a protocol based on the VMEbus specification [ 101 to regulate the bus contention between the CPU and the DMAC. Each device that needs to access the bus sends a bus request first. If the CPU is in a B cycle, the DMAC waits after sending a bus request. The CPU releases the bus when it enters an E cycle. After a short delay, defined as BMT (Bus Mastership Transfer time), the DMAC gains the bus and starts to transfer data. At the end of each transfer of a unit of data, the bus controller checks if there is any bus request from the CPU. The DMAC releases the bus if the CPU is requesting the bus, and the CPU gains the bus after a BMT delay. Otherwise, the DMAC conducts its next transfer.

div.head: The WCET of Basic Structures
div.p: Programs are composed of three basic structures: straight-line structures, loop structures, and conditional structures. Consequently, to bound the WCET of a program executing concurrently with a DMA U 0 operation, we need to bound the WCET of each basic structure when cycle-stealing operations are allowed. We present techniques for bounding the WCET of basic structures in the following subsections. By treating a program as a set of structures, the techniques described in this section comprise a simple approach to bound the WCET of the program. We maintain two global variables in these techniques: W , the variable that returns the WCET of the program, and S, the number of units of data that still need to be transferred.
Initially, we set W to zero and S to the number of units of data required by the DMA I/o operation.

div.head: Loop Structure
div.p: We classify all loop structures into three types shown in Figure 3. A high-level while loop is usually compiled into a type-1 loop structure. Similarly, a repeat and a for loop are usually compiled into a type-2 and a type-3 loop structure, respectively. The variable K in each loop structure is often known as the loop iteration count. It is recognized that the maximum iteration count of a loop structure must be provided in order to bound its WCET.

The Test node in each loop structure is actually a branch instruction. The timing behavior of a branch instruction when the branch is taken is different from when the branch is not taken. Therefore, each branch instruction has two sets of the triple (e, 20,n). In this paper we use Tes t(bran) and Tes t(next) to represent the T e s t node when the branch is taken and when the branch is not taken, respectively. We assume that each loop iteraction count can be bounded. We present in Figure 4 an algorithm that predicts the WCET of a type-1 loop structure. By suitable modifications to the above algorithm, we can obtain the algorithms for type-2 and type-3 loop structures. These algorithms are included in the Appendix (see Figure 6 and Figure 7).

div.head: The Experiment
div.p: Because the concurrent execution of the CPU and the DMAC is allowed, our WCET predictions are expected to be tighter than the pessimistic WCET predictions. To give a quantitative idea about the performance, we designed the following experiment to measure the static and dynamic improvement.

We describe the whole experimental process by the flowchart shown in Figure 5 1 lists the programs we tested in the experiment. Because of the wide use of CPU32 in embedded systems, we used the compiler designed for MC68332, one of the MC68300 Family of embedded controllers, to compile these programs.

We next sent the annotated assembly program to the bus utllization analyzer to calculate its YO bus utilization. The bus utilization analyzer specifically analyzed the worst-case execution path because of its importance in the prediction of the WCET. Assume that there are K 1 E cycles and K2 B cycles in the worst-case execution path. We measure its YO bus utilization by TB Utilization = TB -t TE where TE and TB are the total execution times of K1 E cycles and K2 B cycles, respectively. Because our approach reduces the WCET predictions by utilizing the U 0 bus as much as possible, we expect a greater improvement will be produced on a program with a lower Utilization.

All architectural information needed in the experiment, such as the timing information of each instruction and the I/O bus, is provided in a table-driven manner. The timing information of each instruction, including how many machine cycles the instruction is composed of, the function of each machine cycle, and the execution time of each machine cycle, is obtained from [l]. By assuming that a 0-wait memory is used and the DMA transfer of a unit of data takes 1 bus cycle, we set DT to 120 ns. Finally, we set BMT to 10 ns.

div.head: Conclusion and Future Work
div.p: Cycle-stealing DMA operations have often been disabled in hard-real-time systems because of the difficulty in bounding the interference on an executing program. We presented an analytical method for bounding the WCET of a program which executes concurrently with a cyclestealing DMA U 0 operation. The experimental results demonstrate that a simple approach which implements our analytical method can produce more accurate WCET predictions than the pessimistic approach, especially when the program contains a large percentage of computation intensive instructions.

We developed our analytical method on a machine in which the bus contention is regulated by a protocol based on the VMEbus specification. 4: The results of dynamic experiment sufficiently general, this analytical method is applicable to many other commonly used buses. Because the timing effect of cycle-stealing operations on each instruction is analyzed independently, many techniques, including the language constructs developed by Pusher and Koza [9], the correlation analysis techniques developed by Gupta and Gopinath [2], the semantics-preserving transformation techniques developed by Niehaus [6], and the dynamic path analysis developed by Park [8], can be used to improve the prediction.

To simplify the analysis, we assumed that no cache memory is present. If cache memory is used, the number of bus accesses by the CPU is significantly reduced because of cache hits. We expect a greater improvement due to more accurate accounting for the delay caused by the concurrent execution of cycle-stealing operations. In the future we will extend our analysis to systems in which on-chip cache memory is present.
